q: Which statement about benzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, is true?
c: All six C–C bonds are the same length.
It has three short double bonds and three long single bonds.
It reacts readily with Br<sub>2</sub> by addition, like an alkene.
Each carbon is bonded to two hydrogen atoms.
h: Think about what the circle drawn inside the benzene ring represents.
w: The pi electrons are spread evenly around the ring, so all six C–C bonds are identical, between a single and a double bond in length. That stability is why benzene resists addition reactions; each C has only one H.
x: That describes one drawing of benzene, but its pi electrons are spread over the whole ring. Measured C–C bond lengths do not alternate between short and long.
Alkenes add Br<sub>2</sub> quickly, but benzene does not: addition would break up its stable ring of pi electrons.
Two H on every carbon would be C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub> (cyclohexane). Benzene is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>: six H for six carbons.

q: A benzene ring has a –CH<sub>3</sub> group and a –Cl atom on adjacent carbons. Which name is correct?
h: Use toluene as the parent (the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon is C1), then number to the Cl.
w: With the methyl carbon as C1, an adjacent Cl is on C2: 2-chlorotoluene (ortho-chlorotoluene). 3- and 4- would be meta and para; phenol needs an –OH group.
x: 3- means one ring carbon sits between the –CH<sub>3</sub> and the –Cl (meta). Here the two groups are on neighboring carbons.
4- puts the –Cl directly across the ring from the –CH<sub>3</sub> (para). Here the two groups are on neighboring carbons.
Phenol is the parent name for a ring with an –OH group. This ring has a –CH<sub>3</sub> group instead, which sets a different parent name.

q: Two substituents on a benzene ring are on carbons 1 and 3. This arrangement is called
h: Ortho = neighbors, para = opposite. What is in between?
w: 1,2 is ortho, 1,3 is meta, and 1,4 is para.
x: Ortho means neighboring carbons, 1,2. On carbons 1 and 3 one ring carbon sits between the two substituents.
Para means directly across the ring, 1,4. Carbons 1 and 3 are not opposite each other.
Alpha is not used for positions on a benzene ring. Two groups on a benzene ring are described as ortho, meta or para.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: When a benzene ring is a substituent on a carbon chain, it is called phenyl. Count the chain carbons.
w: The chain has 5 carbons and the C6H5 group sits on C3: 3-phenylpentane. Benzyl would be C6H5CH2–, which is not present here.
x: Benzyl is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–, a ring plus an extra CH<sub>2</sub>. Here the ring is bonded directly to a chain carbon, with no CH<sub>2</sub> in between.
Count from either end: CH<sub>3</sub>, then CH<sub>2</sub>, then the CH that holds the ring. That carbon is not C2.

Count the chain again: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–CH–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> has five carbons, not six. The C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub> carbons belong to the ring substituent, not the main chain.

q: Naphthalene, used in some mothballs, is best described as
c: a benzene ring with a methyl group
a benzene ring with two –OH groups
h: Naphthalene is a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon. What does polycyclic mean?
w: Naphthalene (C10H8) is two benzene rings sharing one side. Larger fused-ring aromatics, such as benzo[a]pyrene in cigarette smoke, are carcinogens.
x: A benzene ring with a methyl group is toluene, C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>8</sub>. Naphthalene is C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, and all ten carbons are in rings.
A six-carbon cycloalkane (cyclohexane) is saturated and not aromatic. Naphthalene is aromatic and has ten carbons.
A benzene ring with two –OH groups is a phenol such as hydroquinone. Naphthalene is a hydrocarbon, C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, with no oxygen.

q: Benzene reacts with Cl<sub>2</sub> in the presence of FeCl<sub>3</sub>. What are the products?
h: Benzene keeps its stable ring: does it add atoms across a double bond or swap an H?
w: Benzene undergoes substitution: one H is replaced by Cl, giving chlorobenzene + HCl. Addition products such as dichlorocyclohexane would destroy the aromatic ring.
x: 1,2-Dichlorocyclohexane has no double bonds left, so the aromatic ring would be gone. Benzene resists losing its ring of pi electrons and does not add Cl<sub>2</sub> the way an alkene does.
Chlorocyclohexane is a saturated ring: all three double bonds would have disappeared. The product of this reaction is still aromatic.
Only one Cl from each Cl<sub>2</sub> ends up on the ring; the other Cl leaves with the H that was displaced. H<sub>2</sub> is not a product.

q: What is the common name of C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, a benzene ring with an amino group?
h: Each common aromatic parent has its own name: –OH, –CH<sub>3</sub> and –NH<sub>2</sub> each have one.
w: C6H5NH2 is aniline. Phenol is C6H5OH, toluene is C6H5CH3 and benzamide is C6H5CONH2.
x: Phenol is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH, a ring with an –OH group, not an –NH<sub>2</sub> group.
Toluene is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, a ring with a methyl group. It has no nitrogen.
Benzamide is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub>: its N is attached to a C=O, which makes an amide. Here the –NH<sub>2</sub> is bonded straight to the ring.

q: 1,4-Dichlorobenzene is used in some toilet-bowl deodorizers. Which name describes the same compound?
h: Ortho = neighbors (1,2), meta = one carbon in between (1,3), para = opposite (1,4).
w: Substituents on carbons 1 and 4 are directly across the ring from each other: para-dichlorobenzene. Cyclohexane is a saturated ring, not benzene.
x: Ortho is 1,2, neighboring carbons. Carbons 1 and 4 are directly across the ring from each other.
Meta is 1,3, with one carbon between the groups. Carbons 1 and 4 have two carbons between them on each side.
Cyclohexane is a saturated ring with no double bonds, so 1,4-dichlorocyclohexane (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>) is a different compound. The question names a benzene ring.

q: A benzene ring carries an –OH group and an –NO<sub>2</sub> group directly across the ring from each other. What is its name?
h: With –OH on the ring, the parent name is phenol. Then decide ortho, meta or para.
w: –OH on benzene makes the parent phenol; groups opposite each other (1,4) are para: p-nitrophenol. Toluene would need a –CH3 instead of –OH.
x: Meta (1,3) has one ring carbon between the two groups. Groups directly across the ring are 1,4.
Ortho (1,2) means the groups are on neighboring carbons, not across the ring.
Toluene is the parent name for a ring with a –CH<sub>3</sub> group. This ring has an –OH group, which sets a different parent name.

q: Nitration of benzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, uses HNO<sub>3</sub> with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> as a catalyst. Which products form?
h: Benzene's ring is very stable, so it keeps all three double bonds. Does it add or substitute?
w: Benzene undergoes substitution, not addition: one ring H is replaced by –NO2, and that H joins the OH from HNO3 as water: C6H5NO2 + H2O (nitrobenzene). Adding HNO3 across a double bond (C6H7NO3) would destroy the aromatic ring.
x: Count oxygens: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + HNO<sub>3</sub> has three O atoms, but C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> has only two. The H removed from the ring pairs up with the OH left over from HNO<sub>3</sub>.
That formula is benzene plus all of HNO<sub>3</sub>, which is what addition across a C=C would give. Benzene's ring resists addition because it would lose its aromatic stability.
That would put an –OH on the ring. HNO<sub>3</sub> with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> attaches the nitrogen to the ring, not an –OH.

q: Benzene, shown, is heated with HNO<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. What is the organic product?
h: Benzene undergoes substitution, not addition: a group replaces one H and the ring stays aromatic.
w: Nitration replaces one ring H with an –NO2 group, giving nitrobenzene + H2O. The ring keeps its three alternating double bonds. Nitrocyclohexane would mean the ring lost its aromaticity; aniline (–NH2) and phenol (–OH) are not formed by nitration.
x: That is aniline, with an –NH<sub>2</sub> group. Nitration attaches an N bonded to two O atoms; turning it into –NH<sub>2</sub> would take a separate reduction step.
That ring has no double bonds left (nitrocyclohexane), so it is no longer aromatic. Nitration of benzene keeps the aromatic ring.
That is phenol, with an –OH group. HNO<sub>3</sub> puts a nitrogen-containing group on the ring, not –OH.

q: Benzene, shown, reacts with Br<sub>2</sub> in the presence of an FeBr<sub>3</sub> catalyst. What is the organic product?
h: Unlike an alkene, benzene keeps its stable ring: Br replaces one H and HBr is the by-product.
w: Aromatic substitution: one H is replaced by Br, giving bromobenzene + HBr. Adding Br2 across a double bond (the dibromo-cyclohexadiene) is what alkenes do, not benzene. Two Br would require a second substitution, and bromocyclohexane has lost all the double bonds.
x: Here Br<sub>2</sub> added across one ring double bond, leaving only two. That is alkene behavior; the benzene ring keeps all three double bonds.
This has two Br atoms on the ring. One Br<sub>2</sub> puts only one Br on the ring; the other Br leaves as HBr with the displaced H.
This ring has no double bonds left (bromocyclohexane), so it is not aromatic. Reaction with Br<sub>2</sub> and FeBr<sub>3</sub> keeps the benzene ring intact.

q: What is the name of the compound shown?
h: Count the ring positions between the two Cl atoms: next to each other (1,2), one apart (1,3), or across the ring (1,4)?
w: The two Cl atoms are on adjacent ring carbons (1,2), which is ortho. Meta is 1,3 and para is 1,4 (directly across). The ring is a benzene ring (alternating double bonds), not cyclohexane, so "dichlorocyclohexane" is wrong.
x: Meta (1,3) would have one ring carbon between the two Cl atoms. Look at the drawing: is there a carbon between them?
Para (1,4) would put the Cl atoms directly across the ring from each other. In the drawing they are not opposite each other.
The ring in the drawing has alternating double bonds, so it is a benzene ring. A cyclohexane ring would have only single bonds.

q: m-Cresol is the preservative that keeps multi-dose insulin vials sterile. It is a phenol with a methyl group on the ring. Which structure is m-cresol?
h: m = meta = 1,3: one ring carbon between the two groups.
w: In m-cresol the –OH and –CH3 are 1,3 on the ring, with one carbon between them. The 1,2 isomer is o-cresol and the 1,4 isomer is p-cresol. Methoxybenzene (anisole) has the same formula, C7H8O, but it is an ether with no –OH, so it is not a phenol at all.
x: Here the –OH and –CH3 are on neighboring carbons (1,2). That is o-cresol; meta needs one ring carbon between them.
Here the –OH and –CH3 are directly across the ring (1,4). That is p-cresol; meta needs one ring carbon between them.
This has an O–CH<sub>3</sub> group (methoxybenzene, an ether) and no –OH. Cresols are phenols, so they need an –OH on the ring.

q: Hydroquinone, shown, is used as a photographic developer and in some prescription creams that fade dark patches of skin (melasma). How are its two –OH groups arranged on the ring?
h: Are the two groups next to each other, one carbon apart, or directly across the ring?
w: The two –OH groups are directly across the ring, 1,4: para. Hydroquinone is p-dihydroxybenzene (benzene-1,4-diol). Trans is a word for alkenes and rings with tetrahedral carbons; benzene rings are flat, so positions on them are named ortho, meta and para instead.
x: Meta (1,3) would leave one ring carbon between the two –OH groups. Look again at where they sit in the drawing.
Ortho (1,2) would put the two –OH groups on neighboring carbons. In the drawing they are farther apart than that.
Cis and trans describe groups on a C=C or on a ring of tetrahedral carbons. Positions on a flat benzene ring are described as ortho, meta or para.

q: Each C–Cl bond is polar. Which compound shown is nonpolar overall?
h: Draw an arrow along each C–Cl bond toward Cl. In which molecule do the arrows point in exactly opposite directions?
w: In para-dichlorobenzene the two C–Cl dipoles point in exactly opposite directions across the flat ring and cancel, so the molecule is nonpolar (dipole moment 0). In the ortho and meta isomers the dipoles are at an angle and only partly cancel. Chlorobenzene has one C–Cl dipole with nothing to cancel it.
x: In this ortho isomer the two C–Cl dipoles are only 60° apart, so they add together instead of cancelling. It is the most polar of the three dichlorobenzenes.
In this meta isomer the two C–Cl dipoles are 120° apart. They partly cancel, but a net dipole remains.
Chlorobenzene has only one C–Cl dipole, with nothing to cancel it, so the molecule is polar.

q: Which compound shown is the most polar (largest dipole moment)?
h: Bond dipoles add like arrows. Two arrows pointing in nearly the same direction give the biggest total.
w: In ortho-dichlorobenzene the two C–Cl dipoles are only 60° apart, so they add up to the largest total (about 2.5 D). In the meta isomer they are 120° apart and partly cancel (about 1.7 D), and in para they cancel completely (0 D). Two polar bonds are not automatically more polar than one: chlorobenzene (1.7 D) beats the para isomer.
x: In this meta isomer the C–Cl dipoles are 120° apart and partly cancel (about 1.7 D). Is there an isomer whose dipoles point more nearly the same way?
In this para isomer the two C–Cl dipoles point in exactly opposite directions and cancel completely: 0 D, nonpolar.
Chlorobenzene's single C–Cl dipole gives about 1.7 D. Two dipoles that point nearly the same way can add up to more than one.

q: The three difluorobenzene isomers I–III are shown. Rank them from most polar to least polar.
h: Identify each as ortho, meta or para. The closer the two C–F dipoles point in the same direction, the larger the total.
w: III is ortho (C–F dipoles 60° apart, add strongly, about 2.5 D), I is meta (120°, partly cancel, about 1.6 D), II is para (180°, cancel to 0 D): III > I > II. Ranking para first assumes groups far apart give a bigger dipole, but opposite arrows cancel.
x: This order is upside down: it puts para first. In para the two C–F dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel to 0 D.
Para is correctly last, but ortho and meta are swapped. Dipoles 60° apart (ortho) add up more than dipoles 120° apart (meta).
Para cannot rank above meta: para dipoles cancel completely (0 D), while meta dipoles only partly cancel.

q: para-Dichlorobenzene, shown, is used in mothballs. Its C–Cl bonds are polar, yet the molecule is nonpolar. Why?
c: The two C–Cl bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.
Carbon and chlorine have the same electronegativity.
The benzene ring is nonpolar, so it cancels any polar bond attached to it.
Chlorine atoms bonded to a ring have no lone pairs.
h: Polarity of a molecule depends on bond polarity AND shape. Where are the two Cl atoms relative to each other?
w: The flat ring holds the two Cl atoms directly across from each other (1,4), so the two equal C–Cl dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel, like CCl4 or CO2. Cl is more electronegative than C, so each bond is polar. The ring does not "cancel" polarity on its own: ortho-dichlorobenzene has the same ring and is polar.
x: Cl (3.0) is more electronegative than C (2.5), so each C–Cl bond is polar, as the question says. The reason must come from how the two bond dipoles are arranged.
A ring cannot cancel a polar bond. ortho-Dichlorobenzene has the same ring and the same two C–Cl bonds, yet it is polar.
A Cl atom bonded to carbon still has three lone pairs. Lone pairs are not what makes this molecule nonpolar.

q: 1,4-Dimethylbenzene (p-xylene) has four equivalent ring H atoms. What is the organic product of the reaction shown?
h: An aromatic ring undergoes substitution, not addition: one ring H is replaced and HBr is the by-product.
w: FeBr3 helps Br replace one ring H, giving 2-bromo-1,4-dimethylbenzene + HBr, and the ring stays aromatic. Adding Br2 across a ring C=C is what alkenes do, not benzene rings. Br on a CH3 group happens with Br2 and light, not FeBr3. Two Br atoms would need a second substitution.
x: Here Br<sub>2</sub> added across a ring double bond, leaving only two. That is alkene behavior; the aromatic ring does substitution instead.
Here Br replaced an H on a CH<sub>3</sub> group. That happens with Br<sub>2</sub> and light, as with alkanes, not with an FeBr<sub>3</sub> catalyst.
This has two Br atoms on the ring. One Br<sub>2</sub> replaces only one ring H; a second Br would need a second substitution.

q: 1,3,5-Trimethylbenzene has three equivalent ring H atoms. What is the organic product of the reaction shown?
h: Nitration replaces one ring H with an –NO<sub>2</sub> group. The methyl groups are not touched.
w: One ring H is replaced by –NO2, giving 1,3,5-trimethyl-2-nitrobenzene + H2O. Nitration substitutes on the ring, not on a CH3 group. An –NH2 group (amine) is not formed by HNO3, and two –NO2 groups would need a second nitration.
x: Here the –NO<sub>2</sub> is on a CH<sub>3</sub> group, not on the ring. HNO<sub>3</sub> with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> replaces a ring H.
This has an –NH<sub>2</sub> group. Nitration attaches an N bonded to two O atoms; –NH<sub>2</sub> would need a separate reduction step.
This has two –NO<sub>2</sub> groups. One nitration replaces only one ring H.

q: Which reagents carry out the conversion shown?
h: The Cl replaced an H on the ring itself. Which conditions substitute on an aromatic ring?
w: Cl2 with an FeCl3 catalyst substitutes Cl for a ring H (HCl is the by-product). Cl2 with light substitutes on the CH3 groups, as it does with alkanes. HCl does not react with a benzene ring, and Br2/FeBr3 would add Br, not Cl.
x: With light, Cl<sub>2</sub> substitutes on the CH<sub>3</sub> groups, as it does with alkanes, not on the ring. Look at where the Cl ends up in the product.
HCl does not react with a benzene ring. Putting a halogen on an aromatic ring takes the halogen itself plus a catalyst.
Br<sub>2</sub> with FeBr<sub>3</sub> does substitute on aromatic rings, but it adds Br. The product shown has Cl.

q: 1,4-Dichlorobenzene is used in mothballs; its four ring H atoms are equivalent. What is the organic product of the reaction shown?
h: Nitration replaces a ring H with –NO2. The Cl atoms and the aromatic ring stay.
w: One ring H is replaced by –NO2: 1,4-dichloro-2-nitrobenzene + H2O. 4-Chloronitrobenzene has the –NO2 replacing a Cl instead of an H. –NH2 is not formed by nitration. Adding H–O and –NO2 across a ring double bond is addition, which the aromatic ring resists.
x: Here –NO<sub>2</sub> replaced one of the Cl atoms, so only one Cl is left. Nitration replaces a ring H, and both Cl atoms stay.
This has an –NH<sub>2</sub> group. Nitration attaches an N bonded to two O atoms; –NH<sub>2</sub> would need a separate reduction step.
Here –OH and –NO<sub>2</sub> added across a ring double bond, leaving only two. The aromatic ring resists addition and does substitution instead.

q: 1,2,4,5-Tetramethylbenzene has two equivalent ring H atoms. What is the organic product of the reaction shown?
h: With FeCl<sub>3</sub>, Cl<sub>2</sub> substitutes on the aromatic ring; HCl is the by-product.
w: Cl replaces one ring H and the ring stays aromatic: 3-chloro-1,2,4,5-tetramethylbenzene + HCl. Adding Cl2 across a ring C=C is alkene behavior. Cl on a CH3 group needs light instead of FeCl3, and replacing both ring H atoms needs a second Cl2.
x: Here Cl<sub>2</sub> added across a ring double bond, leaving only two. That is alkene behavior; the aromatic ring does substitution instead.
Here Cl replaced an H on a CH<sub>3</sub> group. That happens with Cl<sub>2</sub> and light, not with an FeCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst.
Both ring H atoms were replaced here. One Cl<sub>2</sub> replaces only one; this product would need a second Cl<sub>2</sub>.

q: Benzene is drawn below in one of its forms. How many equivalent resonance structures does benzene have?
h: Keep all six carbons in place. In how many ways can the three double bonds alternate around the ring?
w: The three double bonds can sit on either set of alternating ring bonds, giving 2 equivalent structures. That is why benzene is often drawn as a hexagon with a circle inside. 3 counts double bonds; 6 counts carbons.
x: Three is the number of double bonds in each drawing, not the number of resonance structures. In how many ways can three double bonds sit on alternating ring bonds?
One structure would mean the double bonds are fixed in place. Shift every double bond one position around the ring: you get a different but equivalent drawing.
Six is the number of ring carbons. Shifting the double bonds around the ring gives only a few distinct drawings; count them.

q: Isopropylbenzene (cumene) is the starting material for making phenol and acetone. Which structure is isopropylbenzene?
h: An isopropyl group is Y-shaped: the ring is attached to the middle carbon of a three-carbon group.
w: Isopropylbenzene has a three-carbon group bonded to the ring through its middle carbon, –CH(CH3)2. Propylbenzene attaches through the end carbon of a straight chain; 1-ethyl-2-methylbenzene has the same formula but two separate groups; tert-butylbenzene has four carbons in its substituent.
x: This is propylbenzene: the ring is bonded to the end carbon of a straight three-carbon chain. An isopropyl group attaches through its middle carbon.
This has two separate groups on the ring, ethyl and methyl (1-ethyl-2-methylbenzene). Isopropylbenzene has a single three-carbon substituent.
This substituent has four carbons, a central carbon holding three CH3 groups (tert-butyl). An isopropyl group has three carbons.

q: meta-Xylene (1,3-dimethylbenzene) is a solvent in some paints. Pick its drawing.
h: Meta = the two groups have exactly one ring carbon between them (positions 1 and 3).
w: In meta-xylene the two CH3 groups sit on carbons 1 and 3, with one unsubstituted ring carbon between them. Adjacent methyls (1,2) are ortho-xylene; methyls directly across the ring (1,4) are para-xylene. Ethylbenzene is an isomer with a single two-carbon group.
x: Here the two CH3 groups are on neighboring carbons (1,2). That is ortho-xylene.
Here the two CH3 groups are directly across the ring (1,4). That is para-xylene.
This is ethylbenzene, with one two-carbon group. Xylenes have two separate CH<sub>3</sub> groups on the ring.

q: Rank benzene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>), toluene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) and phenol (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH) from highest to lowest boiling point.
h: Which compound can hydrogen bond to itself? Of the two hydrocarbons, which is bigger?
w: Phenol's O–H lets its molecules hydrogen bond to each other, so it boils highest (about 182 °C). Toluene is larger than benzene and has stronger dispersion forces (about 111 °C vs 80 °C). Order: phenol > toluene > benzene.
x: Toluene has only dispersion forces. Phenol's molecules hydrogen bond to one another, which takes more energy to overcome.
This reverses the order. Hydrogen bonding and larger size both raise the boiling point.
Phenol is right at the top, but benzene is smaller than toluene, so benzene has weaker dispersion forces and boils lower.

q: Of these four benzene derivatives, which is the most soluble in water?
h: Which compound has a group that can hydrogen bond with water?
w: Only phenol has an –OH group, which hydrogen bonds with water, so it is moderately soluble. Benzene, toluene and chlorobenzene are almost insoluble because they cannot hydrogen bond with water.
x: Benzene is a nonpolar hydrocarbon. It cannot hydrogen bond with water, so it barely dissolves.
Toluene is a nonpolar hydrocarbon with only dispersion forces, so it is almost insoluble in water.
The C–Cl bond is polar, but chlorobenzene has no H on O or N and cannot donate a hydrogen bond. It is almost insoluble.

q: Naphthalene (C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, two fused benzene rings, once used in mothballs) is a solid at room temperature, while benzene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>) is a liquid. What best explains the difference?
c: Naphthalene is a larger molecule, so its dispersion forces are stronger
Naphthalene molecules hydrogen bond to each other
Benzene is more polar than naphthalene
h: Both are hydrocarbons with only C and H. Which intermolecular force do they have, and what makes it stronger?
w: Both are nonpolar hydrocarbons with only dispersion forces. Naphthalene has more atoms and electrons and a larger flat surface, so its dispersion forces are stronger, and it melts higher (about 80 °C vs about 6 °C for benzene).
x: Hydrogen bonding needs an H on O, N or F. Naphthalene has only C–H bonds.
Naphthalene is a covalent molecule made of C and H only. It contains no ions.
Both are nonpolar hydrocarbons. Polarity does not explain the difference; size does.
